lead: Both readings are about a word that does something. Paul traces the chain by which faith reaches a person: someone is sent, someone proclaims, someone hears, someone believes and calls on the Lord. In Capernaum people hear that word for the first time from the mouth of Jesus, and even an unclean spirit has to obey it. In this season of Denha, the Lord is shown forth by what he says.

r.h: Faith comes from what is heard
set: Romans 9–11 is Paul's long and painful reflection on his own people: how can the Gospel be for all, when many in Israel have not received it? He wrote about their “zeal for God” with love (10:1–2). This reading stands in the middle of that argument. It ends with questions that are carried on into chapter 11, where Paul insists that God has not rejected his people (11:1) and that “the gifts and the calling of God are irrevocable” (11:29).
str: vv. 10–13: believing and confessing; no distinction; all who call will be saved.
vv. 14–15: the chain: call, believe, hear, proclaim, be sent.
vv. 18–20: the word has gone out; Moses and Isaiah on those who were not seeking.
kw: To say the same thing, to declare openly. What the heart believes, the mouth says aloud: “Jesus is Lord” (10:9). Faith is more than private opinion.
The same Greek word means both the act of hearing and the message heard. Faith begins by receiving something from outside ourselves.
The work of a herald, who announces the words of another. The herald does not make up the message, and he has to be sent.
vv: For there is no distinction between Jew and Greek; the same Lord is Lord of all and is generous to all who call on him.
Paul has used the same phrase about sin (3:22–23). The levelling is complete: all need mercy, and it is offered to all.
And how are they to proclaim him unless they are sent? As it is written, “How beautiful are the feet of those who bring good news!”
He quotes Isaiah 52:7, the runner bringing news of God's victory to Jerusalem. Feet, usually dusty and overlooked, are here called beautiful because they have made the journey.
So faith comes from what is heard, and what is heard comes through the word of Christ.
This is the verse's plain teaching: faith has a history. Somebody told us. Each of us stands at the end of a long chain of people who were sent and who spoke.
ch: The Catechism quotes these verses to explain why the Church has an ordained ministry: no one can give himself the mandate to preach the Gospel, for he must be sent (CCC 875). It also teaches that the Church's mission flows from God's will that all be saved (CCC 851), and that God's covenant with the Jewish people has not been revoked (CCC 839).

set: This is the first public act of Jesus in Mark's Gospel, straight after the call of the four fishermen (1:16–20). Capernaum was a fishing town on the north shore of the Sea of Galilee and became his home base (2:1). The synagogue was the place where the community met on the sabbath to hear the Law and the Prophets, and a visiting teacher could be invited to speak.
str: vv. 21–22: he teaches, and they are astounded.
vv. 23–24: the unclean spirit cries out.
vv. 25–26: the rebuke and the expulsion.
vv. 27–28: amazement, and the news spreads.
kw: The word means power that is rightly one's own. A scribe taught by handing on what the teachers before him had said, which was honest and valuable work. Jesus speaks in his own name.
The spirit knows what the crowd does not yet know. Peter uses the same title in John 6:69, but there as a confession of faith. Here it is a cry of fear (compare James 2:19).
Literally “be muzzled”, the word used for an ox in 1 Corinthians 9:9. Jesus does not accept testimony from this source.
vv: They were astounded at his teaching, for he taught them as one having authority, and not as the scribes.
Mark does not yet tell us what he taught. The first thing we learn about the word of Jesus is its effect.
and he cried out, “What have you to do with us, Jesus of Nazareth? Have you come to destroy us? I know who you are, the Holy One of God.”
The “us” is telling. Evil recognizes what this Teacher's coming means. The first to name Jesus in public in this Gospel is his enemy.
But Jesus rebuked him, saying, “Be silent, and come out of him!”
There is no ritual here and no long formula. Only a word. The man himself is not condemned; he is set loose.
He commands even the unclean spirits, and they obey him.
The crowd joins teaching and exorcism: the word that instructs is the same word that releases people. The question “What is this?” will drive the rest of Mark's Gospel.
ch: The Catechism notes that the people were struck by Jesus teaching not as their scribes did (CCC 581), and that his expulsions of demons announce the coming of the Kingdom, the defeat of “the ruler of this world” (CCC 550). The Church continues this work, in the name of Jesus and by his authority, in the prayers of baptism (CCC 1673).

qa: Does “not as the scribes” mean that Jesus looked down on the teachers of Israel?

No. Mark is contrasting two ways of teaching, not judging a whole class of people. Jesus praises a scribe in Mark 12:34 and Matthew speaks of scribes trained for the Kingdom (13:52). The difference lies in who is speaking: the one whose own word has authority.
study: Who first told me about Christ? Have I ever thanked God for that person, or thanked that person?
Paul asks how anyone can hear without someone to proclaim. Is there someone who will hear about Christ only if they hear it from me?
